title: The index can be a variable
idea: The number inside the brackets can be a variable, not just a literal. This connects indexing to the loops from Lap 3. Reviews for + range.

exercises.prompt:
Predict the output:

nums = [3, 7, 2]
i = 1
print(nums[i])
exercises.explanation: i holds 1, so nums[i] is the same as nums[1], which is 7. The index can be any variable that holds a whole number.

exercises.prompt: The number inside the index brackets can come from a variable.
exercises.explanation: Yes. nums[i] uses whatever value i holds as the position. That is what lets a loop walk through a list by index.

exercises.prompt:
Predict the output:

nums = [10, 20, 30]
pos = 2
print(nums[pos])
exercises.explanation: pos is 2, so nums[pos] is nums[2], which is 30. The variable just stands in for the position number.

exercises.prompt:
Recall range from Lap 3. Predict the output:

nums = [5, 6, 7]
for i in range(3):
    print(nums[i])
exercises.explanation: range(3) makes i take 0, 1, 2. Each time, nums[i] gives that position's value: 5, then 6, then 7 — each on its own line.

exercises.prompt: A loop variable from range can be used as a list index.
exercises.explanation: Yes — and that is a big idea. range(3) gives 0, 1, 2, which are exactly the indexes of a three-value list. The loop can visit each one.

exercises.prompt:
Predict the output:

words = ["a", "b", "c"]
for i in range(3):
    print(words[i])
exercises.explanation: i is 0, 1, 2 in turn, so words[i] gives "a", "b", "c" — one word per line. The index variable walks across the positions.

exercises.prompt:
Complete the loop so it prints each value of nums by index:

nums = [8, 9, 10]
for i in range(3):
    print(nums[____])
exercises.explanation: Use the loop variable i as the index: nums[i]. Each pass, i is 0, then 1, then 2, so every value prints in turn.

exercises.prompt: In nums[i], what does the computer do with i FIRST?
options: Look up the value i holds, then use it as the position
exercises.explanation: The computer reads what i currently holds (say 2), then uses that number as the position: nums[2]. The variable is just a stand-in for a number.

exercises.prompt:
Predict the output:

nums = [100, 200, 300]
i = 0
print(nums[i])
i = 2
print(nums[i])
exercises.explanation: First i is 0, so nums[i] is 100. Then i becomes 2, so nums[i] is 300. Changing the index variable changes which value you get.

exercises.prompt: Because range(3) gives 0, 1, 2, it lines up perfectly with the indexes of a 3-value list.
exercises.explanation: Exactly. The positions of a three-value list are 0, 1, 2 — the very numbers range(3) produces. That match is why loops and indexing fit together so well.
